passage:
"So are you going to apply to the science camp?" Jahnavi asked, putting the form on the table.
"Maybe." Akash raised one eyebrow at the paper.
"That's your third maybe this week."
"I know." He picked at the corner of the form. "The others have done coding for years. I'll be the one who doesn't know anything."
"Is it that you don't want to go, or that you're scared it'll go badly?"
He thought about it. "Scared, I think. But also I'm not sure it's even the right camp."
"Both of those are worth looking at. I won't push. Shall we read the syllabus together tonight and list what worries you?"
"Okay." He almost smiled. "Maybe that helps."

qa.q: What does Jahnavi say about Akash's maybe this week?
qa.a: She says it's his third maybe this week.

qa.q: What might Akash be feeling about the science camp?
qa.a: He is probably nervous about not knowing enough compared with the others, and also unsure about whether it suits him, so his doubt mixes fear and careful thinking.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi and Akash do next?
qa.a: They could read the syllabus together and list his worries, sorting the fears from the real questions before he decides.

qa.q: Why might Jahnavi's choice not to push matter to Akash?
qa.a: Pressure could make him feel he had to say yes to please her, while open discussion lets him work out what he really thinks. 🙂

grounding: A teen hesitates and says maybe about a plan, and open discussion works better than pressure.

passage: When Keerthana asked if I'd join the robotics team with her, I said "maybe" and raised one eyebrow, the way I do. She took it as a no. I took it as honest. Truthfully I was arguing with myself: part of me loved the idea, part of me was scared of being the only one who had never soldered anything, and part of me wondered if I was just copying her. She could have called me a coward. Instead she asked, "Which part are you unsure about?" That made me look properly. I said the scared part. Then the doubt started to shrink, because now it had a name and we could talk about it. I joined in the end, but I asked questions first. - Ayesha

qa.q: What did Ayesha say when Keerthana invited her to join the robotics team?
qa.a: She said 'maybe' and raised one eyebrow.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when she said maybe?
qa.a: She was torn, with love for the idea, fear of being the only one who had never soldered anything, and a worry that she was just copying Keerthana.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do that made the doubt easier to handle?
qa.a: She asked which part Ayesha was unsure about, so the doubt could be named and discussed instead of pushed away.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have first read Ayesha's 'maybe'?
qa.a: She took it as a no, which shows that a hesitation can be read in more than one way.

grounding: A teen's maybe and raised brow reflect a mix of fear and careful thinking, and open discussion beats pressure.

subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
passage: In the coaching centre's small classroom, the teacher was solving a probability problem on the board. Pradeep watched the boy in front of him, Chaitanya, who had a frown and had stopped writing. Was he bored? Puzzled? Pradeep couldn't tell. Chaitanya's pen tapped slowly against his page, and once he glanced at the clock. Pradeep almost told the boy beside him that Chaitanya looked bored, but stopped himself. When the teacher let them work alone, Pradeep leaned forward and whispered, "Are you stuck on step three?" Chaitanya let out a breath. "Yes. I've been staring at it for ages and I'm not sure why the number changes." "Same here. Let's ask." They raised their hands together.

qa.q: Which problem was the teacher solving on the board?
qa.a: The teacher was solving a probability problem.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya have been thinking when he frowned and stopped writing?
qa.a: He was probably puzzled about a step he couldn't follow, though a frown and a glance at the clock could also have meant boredom.

qa.q: Why was whispering a question better than telling the other boy that Chaitanya looked bored?
qa.a: The cues were only hints, and asking gave Pradeep the truth; the guess would have been wrong.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt when Pradeep whispered to him?
qa.a: He was probably relieved that someone noticed and that he wasn't alone in being stuck, as his breath out suggests.

grounding: A teen tries to tell whether a classmate is puzzled or bored, treats cues as hints and asks.

subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
passage:
Hi Suraj,
I owe you an apology. During the group study on Thursday I saw you staring out of the window and giving one-word answers, and I told Manoj you were bored and didn't care about the project. I only had your face and your voice, and I filled in the rest myself. Then Kavya said you seemed lost, and I finally asked you outright. You said you hadn't understood the second section and felt awkward saying so. That was very different from what I'd guessed. I'm sorry for calling you bored behind your back. Can we go through the section on Saturday? I'll bring the notes.
Naveen

qa.q: What did Naveen see Suraj doing during the group study?
qa.a: He saw Suraj staring out of the window and giving one-word answers.

qa.q: What was Suraj actually feeling during the study session?
qa.a: He was confused about the second section and awkward about saying so, which was different from the boredom Naveen guessed.

qa.q: What could Naveen do differently next time he isn't sure about someone's attention?
qa.a: He could ask directly and kindly straight away, instead of guessing and telling others.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt if he heard he was called bored?
qa.a: He might have felt misjudged or hurt, since he was actually struggling and shy about it.

grounding: A teen reads a classmate's face and voice as boredom, then learns by asking that it was confusion.

passage: The internet cafe was so loud that Gurleen had to press one finger into her ear. Her phone battery showed six percent, the results page loaded painfully slowly, and Nilesh, sitting beside her, was tapping his knee. When the number finally appeared, Gurleen gasped and froze with her mouth slightly open, staring at the screen. She didn't cheer or cry. She stared as if the words might change. "Gurleen?" Nilesh said. She couldn't answer. He didn't ask again. He just pushed a stray chair out of her way and quietly handed her a glass of water. After a long minute she whispered, "It's higher than I ever expected," and then, finally, laughed.

qa.q: What did Gurleen's phone battery show?
qa.a: It showed six percent.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she froze at the screen?
qa.a: She was astonished, more than merely surprised, and the frozen stare shows she couldn't yet take in the news, which turned out to be joyful.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that helped?
qa.a: He didn't press her to talk and gave her a moment of quiet space with a glass of water until she could speak.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt while waiting for Gurleen to answer?
qa.a: He was probably anxious and unsure whether the news was good or bad, since her frozen face could have meant either.

grounding: A teen gasps and freezes at unexpected results, and a moment of quiet space helps.

passage: Joseph's phone buzzed on the kitchen counter, and the school portal opened as he stood there in his socks. His eyes moved across the marks once, then again. He didn't say anything. His mouth opened a little, his hand stopped halfway to the biscuit tin, and he stood as still as a photograph. The marks were far below what he had expected. His sister Reena, on the sofa, looked up and noticed the silence. She didn't say "what happened" and she didn't say "it's okay." She switched off the television, put the kettle on, and sat quietly at the table. A few minutes later he sat down opposite her and whispered, "I don't get it."

qa.q: Where was Joseph standing when the portal opened?
qa.a: He was standing in the kitchen, in his socks.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling as he stood still with his mouth open?
qa.a: He was astonished and probably distressed, since the marks were far below his expectations and he could not yet say a word.

qa.q: What could Reena do after he says 'I don't get it'?
qa.a: She can listen first, let him talk at his own pace, and help him think about next steps later rather than rushing to fix it.

qa.q: What is it like for Reena watching him freeze?
qa.a: She probably feels worried and unsure what to say, so she chooses quiet company over questions.

grounding: A teen freezes and stares at shocking unexpected results, and a moment of quiet space helps.

subtype: Excited, eager and worried mixed together [Mismatch]
passage: Note from the school trip coordinator. The night before the mountain trip, Vaibhav stayed behind after the briefing. He told me his heart was racing, his stomach felt fluttery, and he couldn't decide whether he was scared or looking forward to it. He asked if something was wrong with him. I told him that eager and nervous often feel the same in the body, and that many people are both at once. I asked him to try saying "I'm excited and a bit worried" out loud, and he did, twice. His shoulders came down. I suggested he pack his bag with his roommate to keep his hands busy, and I'll check on him at breakfast. - Yamini

qa.q: When did Vaibhav stay behind after the briefing?
qa.a: He stayed behind the night before the mountain trip.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling before the trip?
qa.a: He was both eager and worried at once; the racing heart and fluttery stomach fit either feeling, and he could not tell which it was.

qa.q: How did naming the feeling help him?
qa.a: Saying 'I'm excited and a bit worried' out loud gave the nervous energy a label, which relaxed his shoulders and turned it toward readiness.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt hearing Vaibhav ask if something was wrong with him?
qa.a: She was probably concerned and reassuring, since she explained that the mix is common and kept an eye on him.

grounding: A teen before a trip feels eager and anxious at once with the same racing heart, and labelling it as excitement helps.

subtype: Excited, eager and worried mixed together [Mismatch]
passage: Sunday night. Interview tomorrow at the bakery, my first ever. My heart's been racing for an hour, my hands are cold, and I keep going over my answers. I told Gurpreet on the phone that I felt sick with fear. She said, "Are you sure it isn't excitement in disguise? Your heart does the exact same thing at the fair." That stopped me. I checked: I do want the job, I've been imagining wearing the apron. So I said aloud, "I'm nervous and excited." Weirdly, the racing feels more like fuel now. Still a bit scared of forgetting my words, but I laid out my clothes and I think I'm ready. 😅 - Madhuri

qa.q: Where is Madhuri's interview?
qa.a: Her interview is at the bakery.

qa.q: What is Madhuri feeling as she talks with Gurpreet?
qa.a: She is nervous and excited together, and when she checked, she realised she really wants the job as well as fearing forgetting her words.

qa.q: How can Madhuri use the racing heart tomorrow?
qa.a: She can remind herself that the racing is energy getting her ready and name it as excitement and nerves, then breathe and start her first answer.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's comment have helped Madhuri see it differently?
qa.a: By comparing it to the fair, Gurpreet showed that the same racing heart can go with fun, which made the fear less alarming.

grounding: A teen before a first interview feels eager and worried with the same racing heart, and labelling it as excitement helps.

passage: The final point came as the last light faded and the first raindrops hit the kabaddi ground. Kamal's team had won by a single raid. He punched the air, roared, and was swallowed by teammates hugging him and thumping his back. It felt wonderful, like something huge had lifted off his chest. Then he saw Rukmini, the rival captain, standing alone with her hands on her knees, soaked and not looking up. He heard himself stop shouting. With the rain coming harder and the crowd already heading for shelter, he walked across the wet mud and held out his hand. "That was the toughest match we've had. You were brilliant." She shook it, smiling a little.

qa.q: What happened as the last light faded?
qa.a: The first raindrops hit the kabaddi ground as Kamal's team won by a single raid.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when he saw Rukmini standing alone?
qa.a: He was still full of joy, but noticing her disappointment made him stop shouting and feel some care for her.

qa.q: Why was crossing the muddy ground to shake her hand a good choice?
qa.a: It shared his triumph graciously and avoided gloating, which could have hurt Rukmini more.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt when Kamal offered his hand?
qa.a: She was probably disappointed about losing, but touched by the respect, and her small smile suggests some comfort.

grounding: A teen cheers and hugs teammates after a win and shares the triumph graciously with the rival.

passage: "Yes! Yes! Three-two!" Abhinav yelled across the school quad, arms raised, as his house team stormed him in a heap. The inter-house football win was the best afternoon of his year. He jumped on a bench, pointed at the losing side and sang, "Who's the champion now?" A few of his teammates laughed. Then he saw Irfan, his friend since Class 6, sitting on the grass with his shirt pulled over his knees, staring at nothing. Abhinav's chest felt suddenly heavy. He climbed down, walked over and sat beside him. "That last goal was lucky," he said. "Your defence was really strong. Sorry about the singing." Irfan shrugged, but he moved over to make room.

qa.q: What was the score of the football match?
qa.a: The score was three-two.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he saw Irfan sitting on the grass?
qa.a: His joy was mixed with regret and concern, and his heavy chest suggests he realised his gloating had hurt a friend.

qa.q: What could Abhinav do after sitting down to keep the friendship strong?
qa.a: He could keep listening, avoid further gloating, and maybe suggest a friendly match later, showing that the friendship matters more than the win.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt while Abhinav sang on the bench?
qa.a: He may have felt stung and small, since the song was aimed at his team, though he left room on the grass for Abhinav afterwards.

grounding: A teen celebrates a win with fist pumps and hugs, and learns that gloating can hurt while sharing it graciously helps.

passage: At the village tea stall, Tushar took his tea, looked at Ganga's new haircut without any expression, and said, "Very bold. Did the buffalo help?" Nobody laughed. Ganga's hand went to her hair. His face was as flat as a slate, and the tea seller stopped stirring. Tushar sipped and waited. Ganga couldn't tell whether he meant it kindly or cruelly. Three weeks ago she wouldn't have hesitated, because they had known each other forever, but he'd been teasing everyone lately. "Tushar, are you joking?" she asked. A tiny twitch appeared at the corner of his mouth. "Obviously. It looks good. I'm just bad at compliments." She let out her breath and laughed.

qa.q: What did Tushar ask about Ganga's haircut?
qa.a: He asked, 'Did the buffalo help?'

qa.q: What was Ganga thinking when Tushar said it without any expression?
qa.a: She was unsure whether it was a joke or an insult; the flat face gave her nothing to go on, and she felt worried about her hair.

qa.q: What could Tushar do so his deadpan jokes don't hurt?
qa.a: He could add a small signal like a smile or check that the other person is in on it, especially when they can't tell.

qa.q: How might the tea seller have read the moment?
qa.a: The tea seller stopped stirring, so they may have been unsure too, since deadpan needs shared understanding and an onlooker doesn't have it.

grounding: A teen delivers a joke or insult with no expression, listeners can't tell if it's humour, and asking settles it.

passage: In the school canteen in Addis Ababa, Yara finished her class presentation and sat down with her lunch, still shaky. Abebe leaned over the table, face perfectly still, and said, "Your presentation was the longest ten minutes of my life." Yara froze with her fork in the air. His eyes gave nothing away. Other boys at the next table looked up. She felt her cheeks heat, because she had worked hard on it. Then she remembered how he talked to his brother, the same dry voice. "Is that a joke, Abebe, or do you mean it?" He blinked. "A joke. I couldn't stop watching. I'm sorry, I should smile when I do that." Yara laughed a little unsteadily.

qa.q: Where were Abebe and Yara when he spoke?
qa.a: They were in the school canteen in Addis Ababa.

qa.q: What might Yara be feeling when Abebe says her presentation was the longest ten minutes of his life?
qa.a: She might feel hurt and embarrassed, since she worked hard and his face showed nothing, but she is also unsure whether it was a joke.

qa.q: What could Abebe do differently next time?
qa.a: He could add a smile or a warm word to show he is joking, or say it in private, since his deadpan style needs shared understanding.

qa.q: How might the boys at the next table see the exchange?
qa.a: They may see a joke or an insult, depending on what they know of Abebe, and they don't have Yara's history with his dry voice.

grounding: A teen's deadpan joke lands as possible insult, and asking settles it, since deadpan needs shared understanding.

passage: For about a month last year I answered everything in single words. "Fine." "Okay." "Nothing." I sat with my phone at meals and stared at it even when nothing was on the screen. Nobody could tell why, and honestly neither could I. I was tired, because I'd been sleeping badly, and I was hurt about a fight with my friend Dev, and mostly I didn't want to talk about it. My sister Leela didn't accuse me of being rude. She put a plate of mango beside me and said, "No need to talk, I'm just here." She did that for weeks. One evening, out of nowhere, I told her everything. She only said "thank you for telling me." - Chetan

qa.q: What did Chetan sit with at meals?
qa.a: He sat with his phone at meals.

qa.q: What might Chetan have been feeling during that month?
qa.a: He felt tired and hurt about the fight with his friend Dev, and he didn't want to talk, so his single words covered several feelings at once.

qa.q: What did Leela do that helped?
qa.a: She didn't accuse him, stayed nearby and checked in patiently over weeks, so he could talk when he was ready.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt during those weeks?
qa.a: She may have felt worried and unsure whether her quiet care was working, but she kept showing up.

grounding: A teen who withdraws, answers in single words and stares at a screen has several causes, and patient check-ins help.

passage: Form tutor's note. Over the last three weeks Jeevan's behaviour in class has changed. He arrives late, answers in single words, and stares at his phone under the desk in the breaks instead of sitting with his friends. He isn't rude and he isn't in trouble; he just seems far away. I don't know the reason. It could be tiredness, a problem at home, hurt feelings with a friend or simply a dull stretch. I haven't confronted him. Instead I say good morning each day and ask one easy question, such as how football went. Yesterday he answered with a full sentence. I'll keep checking in over the coming weeks. - Anirban

qa.q: How long has Jeevan's behaviour been different?
qa.a: It has changed over the last three weeks.

qa.q: What might Jeevan be feeling behind his single words and phone use?
qa.a: It could be tiredness, worry about something at home, hurt with a friend or plain boredom, and Anirban admits he doesn't know which.

qa.q: Why did Anirban choose easy daily questions over confronting Jeevan?
qa.a: Detachment has many causes, so accusing him could make him withdraw further, while patient small check-ins keep the door open.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see Anirban's good mornings?
qa.a: He may feel noticed without being pressured, and the full sentence yesterday suggests he is beginning to feel a little safer.

grounding: A teen who withdraws and stares at a screen may be tired, hurt or bored, and patient check-ins are better than accusations.

passage:
Dear Arohi didi,
You asked why my face was so blank at the school prize day. Honestly, I was so happy about my art prize that I was scared I'd cry in front of everyone, so I made my face stone. Last week when Riya laughed at my drawing, I did the same, to hide that it hurt. It works: nobody sees anything. But then nobody asks either, and sometimes I want them to. At home I'm not sure how to switch it off. Could you ask me a question once in a while, when we're on the terrace, and not push? I think I'd answer you.
Love, Hansa

qa.q: What prize did Hansa win?
qa.a: She won an art prize.

qa.q: Why did Hansa keep her face blank on prize day and last week?
qa.a: She wanted to avoid showing too much joy or hurt in front of others, which protects her privacy though it also hides what she needs.

qa.q: What does Hansa ask her cousin to do?
qa.a: She asks Arohi didi to ask her a question once in a while on the terrace, without pushing, so she has a chance to talk.

qa.q: How might Arohi see a blank face like Hansa's?
qa.a: She might not know whether Hansa is happy or hurt, so she may need to offer chances to talk instead of trying to read it.

grounding: A teen keeps a blank face to avoid showing hurt or joy to peers, which protects privacy but can hide need.

passage: Dilnaz, you asked how I became the girl who never reacts. It started in the hostel. First year, some girls laughed at my accent, and I noticed that when I looked upset, they laughed more. So I practised: no frown, no smile, nothing. By the second week I was good at it. Zeenat the statue, that's what they called me. It kept me safe. The problem is that I did the same when I got selected for the debate team, and no one knew I was thrilled. My roommate Sana finally put a cup of chai on my desk and said, "You don't have to show me anything. I'm just here if you want to say." I did, a week later.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat start keeping a blank face in the hostel?
qa.a: Some girls laughed at her accent and laughed more when she looked upset, so she learned to show nothing.

qa.q: What might Zeenat have been feeling when she was selected for the debate team?
qa.a: She felt thrilled, but her blank face hid it, so nobody knew.

qa.q: What did Sana do that helped Zeenat open up?
qa.a: She put chai on the desk and offered to listen without demanding anything, giving Zeenat a chance to talk when ready.

qa.q: How might Sana have felt about Zeenat's blank face?
qa.a: She may have felt unsure whether Zeenat needed help, which is why she waited and offered quietly instead of insisting.

grounding: A teen keeps a blank face to avoid showing hurt or joy, protecting privacy but hiding need until someone offers a chance to talk.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Uday, since you asked about my blushing: it's the worst in assembly. Last term, the teacher asked me to read the morning thought. As soon as I walked to the microphone my face went hot, and I was sure that the whole hall was staring at my red cheeks. My heart was banging. What helped was small things. I breathed out slowly, longer than I breathed in. I looked at the page and at the back wall instead of watching myself in my head. And I reminded myself that most people are thinking about their own morning, not my face. I still turned red, and I read all the same. I'm Pallavi, by the way. Afterwards nobody said a word about it.

qa.q: Where is the blushing the worst for Pallavi?
qa.a: It is the worst in assembly.

qa.q: What was Pallavi afraid of at the microphone?
qa.a: She was afraid the whole hall was staring at her red cheeks, which fed her anxiety and her banging heart.

qa.q: What steps helped Pallavi when she blushed?
qa.a: She breathed out slowly, looked at the page and the back wall, and reminded herself that most people were thinking about their own morning.

qa.q: How might the students in the hall have seen her?
qa.a: Most were probably busy with their own thoughts, so they likely didn't notice her blush as much as she feared.

grounding: A teen who blushes easily fears being noticed, and slow breathing, focusing outward and remembering most people don't notice help.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Payal got asked a question in biology, and I was sitting right behind her. She went red from her collar up to her ears. I saw her put down her pen and take one long breath out, then another. She looked at the diagram on the board rather than at anyone, and I heard her say, "Could you repeat the question, Miss?" Her voice was small but steady. She answered correctly. Afterwards she pressed the back of her hand to her cheek and gave a short laugh. I can't tell if she was frightened, or just hot, or embarrassed. She seemed to calm down after a bit. Nobody around us even glanced at her. - Indu

qa.q: What did Payal ask the teacher after she was called on?
qa.a: She asked the teacher to repeat the question.

qa.q: What might Payal have been feeling when she blushed?
qa.a: She was probably anxious about being looked at, shown by the long breaths and looking at the board, though Indu admits it could also have been heat or embarrassment.

qa.q: What helped Payal steady herself?
qa.a: Slow breaths and focusing on the diagram instead of the faces around her.

qa.q: How did the other students seem to see Payal's blush?
qa.a: Indu notes that nobody around them even glanced at her, which fits the idea that most people don't notice as much as the blusher fears.

grounding: A teen who blushes easily fears being noticed, and slow breathing and focusing outward help.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: In the school library, Preeti looked up from her book and saw Vijay at the far table with wet cheeks and a letter in his hand. Her first thought was that someone had upset him. She walked over, but kept her distance. "Hey. Are you okay? I can sit or go, whichever you like." He wiped his eyes with his sleeve and half laughed. "Sit. I'm fine. I just got the scholarship letter. I didn't think I'd get it, and I can't stop crying." Preeti smiled and pulled out the chair. She noticed her first guess was completely wrong. "Congratulations, then." "Thanks. It's odd, I'm so happy that my eyes won't stop leaking."

qa.q: Where was Vijay sitting when Preeti saw him?
qa.a: He was at the far table in the school library.

qa.q: What might Vijay be feeling, and what was Preeti's first guess?
qa.a: Vijay is relieved and very happy about the scholarship letter, while Preeti first guessed that someone had upset him.

qa.q: Why was Preeti's gentle question better than assuming?
qa.a: Tears can mean sadness, anger, stress, laughter or relief, so asking and staying present let her learn the truth.

qa.q: How might Vijay have felt when Preeti offered to sit or go?
qa.a: He probably felt cared for and free to choose, since she didn't push him and let him decide. 🙂

grounding: A teen reads a friend's tears and guesses sadness, but tears also come from relief, so asking gently is wiser.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
Hi Binita,
I want to say sorry about yesterday. When I saw you at the bus stop with tears running down your face, I decided you must be sad, and I started saying "oh no, don't cry, it'll be fine" in my softest voice. You looked at me as if I'd got it wrong. Then you told me you weren't sad at all, you were furious about the comment someone made in class, and the tears just came out. That was a completely different feeling, and my comforting had missed. Next time I'll ask what's going on before I decide. I stayed with you until the bus came, and I'm glad I did. Text me if you want to talk more.
Tenzin

qa.q: Where did Tenzin see Binita crying?
qa.a: He saw her at the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Binita actually feeling when the tears came?
qa.a: She was furious about a comment someone made in class, and the tears came out of anger, not sadness.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do next time he sees a friend crying?
qa.a: Ask gently what is going on and stay nearby, instead of deciding the cause and comforting the wrong feeling.

qa.q: How might Binita have felt when Tenzin said 'oh no, don't cry, it'll be fine'?
qa.a: She might have felt misunderstood, since her anger was being treated as sadness, but she may also have appreciated that he cared enough to stay.

grounding: A teen reads a friend's tears as sadness, then learns they came from anger, so asking gently is wiser.
